notes:
What's new in 0.3.0:

- Full rewrite is working again. If you use Full rewrite to turn your dictations into clean prose, you've probably noticed it stopped working — your words got only the basic cleanup, and you saw the "Full rewrite unavailable" notice. The cloud model Dicta was set up to call got retired, so every request failed. You didn't do anything wrong and there's no setting to fix. Dicta now points to a current model that polishes text the same way and at the same speed.
- Dicta keeps only one copy running at a time, so your words don't paste twice. When you had more than one copy of Dicta open, a single dictation got pasted twice into your app — the words landed duplicated, right next to each other. Now Dicta makes sure only one copy runs per session. If a second copy tries to start, it notices the first one, closes itself right away, and leaves a note in the log. You don't have to close anything manually or change any settings.
- Dicta now tells you when something goes wrong instead of failing silently. A small panel appears above your work with a Dismiss button and disappears on its own after 15 seconds — it never takes keyboard focus away from the app you're typing into. It speaks up when your microphone is unavailable or gets unplugged mid-dictation, when the speech model isn't ready yet, when transcription fails, when Full rewrite can't reach its service and falls back to cleanup, when an administrator window blocks the Dicta shortcut (and tells you how to fix it), or when typed text fails to land in your app. The same problem won't nag you repeatedly — each one speaks up again independently after it clears.
- Your spoken words now survive a crash. Dicta saves the audio on your PC before it starts listening, so a crash or a failed transcription no longer loses what you said. A dictation that had trouble appears in History marked unfinished with a Re-transcribe button that runs it again from the saved audio, or says the audio is unavailable if the recording is already gone. A crash-interrupted dictation is picked up and marked when you launch next time. You control how long Dicta keeps the audio in Settings under "Keep audio recordings": Off, 1 day, 7 days (the default), 30 days, or Forever. The recordings stay on your PC, are never uploaded, and are deleted when you delete that history entry or clear all history.
- The Dictionary tab's free-text "Corrections" box is now an ordered list of rules. You can reorder them, switch a rule off without deleting it, and add or remove rules individually. Rules run in your order, match whole words only and ignore case, and a rule's output is never fed into another — so "dog becomes wolf" and "wolf becomes bear" gives you wolf, not bear. Your existing corrections carry over automatically the first time. These rules now also apply when Full rewrite is switched on, not just to plain cleanup as they did before.
- When you correct yourself out loud mid-sentence, Dicta now types only what you meant. Say "let's meet Tuesday, I mean Wednesday" and it types the Wednesday version, dropping the words you took back. It handles the English cues — "I mean", "no wait", "actually make that" — and the Spanish ones — "digo", "mejor dicho", "o sea no" — and it also removes a false start where you begin the same phrase twice. It deliberately leaves ambiguous phrasing alone — "what I mean is", "no, wait for me", ordinary conversational uses — rather than guessing and deleting words you meant to keep. This runs before Dicta formats numbers and lists, and before Full rewrite.
